# Goals of This Section

## Goals of This Section

Today we will:

- Discuss trends in male-female earnings differentials in Canada
- Introduce taste-based and statistical discrimination theories
- Explain supply-side and non-competitive theories of discrimination
- Learn the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to measure discrimination
- Review policies to address gender discrimination

# Introduction

## Male and Female Earnings

![](images/Screenshot%202025-11-19%20at%2011.43.43%20AM.png){fig-align="center"}

## Male and Female Earnings

![](images/gendergapbygroup.png){fig-align="center"}

## Male and Female Earnings

![](images/gendergapbach.png){fig-align="center"}

## Male and Female Earnings

- Clearly men and women earn different amounts on average
- There are [two broad explanations]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} for this gap:
  1. [Differences in characteristics]{.fg style="color: #555;"} (education, experience, occupation, industry, hours worked, etc.)
  2. [Differences in returns to those characteristics]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} (discrimination)
- Our models so far have not left room for discrimination
  - We treated all workers as the same
  - So there should not be any differences in returns

## Male and Female Earnings

In this section, we explore [economic theories of discrimination]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}:

- Can come from [employers, customers, co-workers]{.fg style="color: #555;"}
- Can be [statistical or taste-based]{.fg style="color: #555;"}

Estimating discrimination empirically is difficult:

- Need to control for all relevant characteristics
- Need to separate differences in characteristics from differences in returns

## Male and Female Earnings

Methods that can help:

- [Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- [Audit studies]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- [Field experiments]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

# Demand Theories of Discrimination

## Demand-Side Theories

[Demand-side theories]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} focus on the behaviour of employers in demanding labour. Discrimination can happen for various reasons:

- Pure prejudice against female workers
- Customer preference to buy from male workers
- Male workers' aversion to working with women

::: {.callout-warning}
These all cause a fall in the [demand for women]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} relative to men in the labour market — reducing wages and employment of female workers
:::

## Taste-Based Discrimination

::: {.callout-important}
## Becker (1957)
[Taste-based discrimination:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} employers have a "taste" for discrimination — they behave as if hiring women is more costly than it actually is
:::

- Firms produce according to: $y = f(N_m + N_w)$
- In a competitive market, profits are:
  $$ \pi = p \cdot f(N_m + N_w) - w_m N_m - w_w N_w $$
- Firms do not maximize profit strictly, but instead maximize:
  $$ U = \pi - d \cdot N_w $$
  - $d$ measures the [degree of discrimination]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - If $d = 0$: no discrimination; if $d > 0$: firms get disutility from hiring women

## Taste-Based Discrimination

The first order conditions for utility maximization are:

$$ p \cdot MP_{N_m} = w_m $$
$$ p \cdot MP_{N_w} = w_w + d $$

- For both men and women, firms hire up to where VMP equals the [effective cost]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} of hiring
- But for women, there is an [additional cost $d$]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} due to discrimination
- If $w_m = w_f$ and men and women are equally productive, this implies firms hire [fewer women]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - Discrimination drives a wedge between wages and the MRP

## Taste-Based Discrimination

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/flabour.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Graph plots labour demand for women
- [Discrimination shifts demand curve left]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- Without discrimination: firm hires where $w_f = MRP_{ND}$
- With discrimination: firm hires where $w_f + d = MRP_D$
  - Or equivalently $w_f = MRP_D - d$
- Implies a [lower level of female labour]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
:::
::::::

## Taste-Based Discrimination

- Above analysis is for a single employer
- Employers discriminate along a spectrum — some have a high $d$, some have a low or no $d$
- Suppose women are able to seek out the [non-discriminating employers]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- If we order firms from lowest to highest by the amount of discrimination:
  - We can get the market demand curve by summing individual demand curves horizontally
- This demand curve is plotted on the next slide

## Taste-Based Discrimination

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/flabour_mkt.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- Vertical axis is the ratio of female to male wages
- For [non-discriminating firms]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}, this ratio is 1
  - A certain set of firms will hire women at this ratio (flat portion of demand curve)
- As the supply of women grows, they must work at [more discriminating firms]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - These firms will only hire when the wage ratio falls
:::
::::::

## Taste-Based Discrimination

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/flabour_mkt_supp.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- If the supply of female labour is [small enough]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}, they can work at non-discriminating firms
  - Wage ratio is 1
- With a [larger supply]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}, some will have to work at discriminating firms
  - Wage ratio falls below 1
  - This is where the demand curve slopes downwards
  - [Wage gap emerges]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
:::
::::::

## Statistical Discrimination

::: {.callout-important}
## Statistical Discrimination
[Statistical discrimination:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} firms use group characteristics to infer individual productivity

- Arises because of [imperfect information]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} — employers do not know individual worker productivity perfectly
- Instead they use signals to infer worker quality
- If one group has lower average productivity (or a noisier signal), firms may pay them less on average
:::

- Contrast with [taste-based discrimination]{.fg style="color: #555;"}, which relies on employers having overt prejudice

## Statistical Discrimination

## Theory

Assume that the abilities of male and female workers are distributed with means $\bar{a}_{m}$ and $\bar{a}_{f}$. The firm has access to a signal of ability $x$ for each person. Expected ability is:

$$a(x) = \bar{a} + \alpha (x - \bar{a})$$

Where $\alpha$ is the [reliability of the signal]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}:

- If $\alpha = 0$: the signal provides no information beyond the average
- If $\alpha = 1$: the signal is perfectly informative

Workers are paid a wage equal to their marginal revenue product

## Statistical Discrimination

Paying workers their marginal revenue product implies:

$$w(x) = p a(x) = p \bar{a} + p \alpha (x - \bar{a})$$

Assume $\bar{a}_{m} = \bar{a}_{f}$ (men and women are equally productive on average), but the signal is [more reliable for men]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}: $\alpha_m > \alpha_f$

Differences arise between workers who score the same on the signal:

- If a man and woman score above average ($x - \bar{a} > 0$), then [men are paid more]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- If a man and woman score below average ($x - \bar{a} < 0$), then [women are paid more]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}

## Statistical Discrimination

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/clipboard-2063601146.png)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- [Male line is steeper]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} because the signal is more reliable ($\alpha_m > \alpha_f$)
- For test scores [above average]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}: men are paid more
- For test scores [below average]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}: women are paid more
- At the average: they are paid the same
:::
::::::

## Statistical Discrimination

- There are no underlying differences between males and females
  - Differences in wages arise because of [differences in the quality of the signal]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - Firms place more weight on average ability for female workers
  - Firms place more weight on the actual signal for male workers
- But where does the assumption $\alpha_m > \alpha_f$ come from?
  - Possibly related to prejudicial attitudes of firms
  - Some believe standardized tests favour males

## Statistical Discrimination

- There may also be differences in $\bar{a}_m$ and $\bar{a}_f$
  - Possibly due to [pre-market discrimination]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} leading to lower human capital among women
- In this case, males are paid more at [every signal level]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- Wage differences do not necessarily arise from overt discrimination
  - They may originate in differences in information signals or average productivity
  - But it is difficult to explain why such differences in signal quality exist

## Statistical Discrimination

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/clipboard-2338105223.png)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
- In this graph the quality of the signal is the same (equal slopes)
- But there are [differences in average productivity]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - Male line lies above female line
- Men will be paid more because of the average difference
:::
::::::

# Supply Theories of Discrimination

## Supply-Side Theories

- We discussed demand-side theories — focused on employer behaviour
- [Discrimination may also arise on the labour supply side]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Factors that affect where women choose or are able to work

## Crowding Hypothesis

::: {.callout-note}
## Crowding Hypothesis
Women are [overrepresented in certain occupations]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}, pushing up their labour supply in those occupations — which [depresses wages]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} relative to men

- Women are paid their marginal product
- But are corralled into a small set of jobs, which depresses wages
:::

## Dual Labour Market Theory

::: {.callout-important}
## Dual Labour Market Theory
There are two distinct labour markets:

- [Primary market:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} high wages, good working conditions, opportunities for advancement; unionized, stable, expanding
- [Secondary market:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} low wages, poor working conditions, little opportunity for advancement; non-unionized, highly competitive, declining
:::

Theory posits that women are concentrated in the secondary market — prejudice prevents women from entering the primary market

## Lower Reservation Wages

Theory: female reservation wages are lower because:

- Costly to search for non-discriminating employers
- Job search is limited by strong household ties
- Ability to negotiate higher pay limited by lower threat of leaving

::: {.callout-note}
With a lower reservation wage, women are more likely to be paid less — contributing to the pay gap

Some empirical evidence supports this
:::

## Risk Aversion

- Large literature documenting that women are less aggressive/competitive in bargaining
  - Also less confident in their abilities
  - Evidence of this in many studies in economics and psychology
- Might mean women are [less likely to compete for higher paying jobs]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

## Differences in Preferences

May be differences in preferences for education, training, hours, work conditions, occupation — all of these are correlated with pay

::: {.callout-warning}
## The Endogeneity Problem
These choices are sometimes a product of discrimination — so it is [hard to separate preferences from discrimination effects]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

Example: STEM fields pay well, but are male dominated — history of discrimination in this field may lead women not to choose it
:::

# Non-Competitive Theories of Discrimination

## Non-Competitive Theories

- One issue with the above theories: they assume [competitive markets]{.fg style="color: #555;"}
- Men and women are assumed to have equal productivity
- Discriminating firms hire fewer women because of prejudice
- But non-discriminating firms can hire more women at lower wages
  - Would [increase their profits]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
  - Non-discriminating firms would bid up wages of women
  - Should [close the gap]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}

## Non-Competitive Theories

::: {.callout-note}
## Why Does the Gap Persist?
Non-competitive theories explain persistent wage gaps when markets are not perfectly competitive — due to monopsony power, imperfect information, search frictions, etc.
:::

## Imperfect Information

- Even if firms know they can increase profits by hiring more women, they might not be able to immediately change their workforce
  - Hiring and recruiting are [costly]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} — search frictions, quasi-fixed costs
- Firms may be slow to adjust to profit opportunities
- This can lead to [persistent wage gaps]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - But does not explain why the gaps have persisted for so long

## Queueing Theory

- Some firms pay [efficiency wages]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Wages above the market clearing level to increase productivity
- This results in a [queue of workers]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} wanting to work at the firm
- While rationing jobs, firms may discriminate

## Political Pressure

- Sometimes market decisions are overridden by political pressures
- A male-centric government or union may:
  - Hire more men in government jobs
  - Be discriminatory with education and training
- The political pressure could come from [interest groups]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - May have significant resources to lobby the government

## Monopsony Power

- Monopsony gives firms power to [set wages below competitive levels]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- Monopsonies may take advantage of the [relative immobility of women]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} to lower their wages
  - Recall women may have stronger ties to household
- They may also try to pit men and women against each other
  - Create competition between the groups to lower wages

## Systemic Discrimination

::: {.callout-note}
## Systemic Discrimination
Discrimination is embedded in social and economic systems — has been going on for so long that it is now [self-perpetuating]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

Could come from:

- Existence of "old boys" mentality
- Old job requirements that implicitly discriminate but continue to exist
:::

# Productivity Differences

## Productivity Differences

- It may be the case that men and women have [productivity differences]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - This could determine pay differences even in competitive markets
- Note: not *innate* productivity differences
- Differences coming from [acquisition of human capital]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} over time:
  - Education
  - Training
  - Work experience
- If human capital investments are a choice, then pay differences are [not discrimination]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- But it could be that choices are [influenced by discrimination]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

## Dual Role

- Traditionally women have more of a [dual role]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} than men — balancing household and market work
- If this continues to be true, then women:
  - Have less continuity in work (mainly from interruptions for children)
  - Are more likely to have periods of paid work and labour force withdrawals
- This leads to [lower accumulation of human capital]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - Because there is less time to recoup the costs
- In some sense this is a rational choice — but is rooted in a society that does not accommodate enough for working mothers

## Pre-Market Discrimination

::: {.callout-important}
## Pre-Market Discrimination
[Pre-market discrimination:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} discrimination that influences choices before workers even enter the labour market

- Education
- Training
- Career path

What looks like a rational choice is itself affected by discrimination
:::

Example: STEM jobs pay well but are male dominated — women are discouraged from entering these fields, and thus do not have access to the higher pay that comes with them

# Measuring Discrimination

## Introduction

- Now that we have discussed theories of discrimination, how do we [measure it]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}?
- Difficult because in most cases discrimination is [not directly observable]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - There is no "discrimination" variable in datasets
- Can design experiments to measure discrimination:
  - [Audit studies]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - [Field experiments]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- But in most cases we have to rely on [observational data]{.fg style="color: #555;"}

## Introduction

- Measuring discrimination involves comparing people of [equal productivity]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - So that any leftover wage differences could be due to discrimination
- But we do not observe productivity directly
- Instead, hold constant variables related to productivity:
  - Education
  - Experience
  - Occupation
  - Industry
  - Hours worked
- Then [decompose the wage difference]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} into part due to characteristics and part due to other factors

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

::: {.callout-important}
## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition
Method to decompose differences in average earnings between two groups into:

- [Explained part:]{.fg style="color: #555;"} due to differences in characteristics (endowments)
- [Unexplained part:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} due to differences in returns to those characteristics (potentially discrimination)
:::

Suppose we estimate a regression of log earnings on observed characteristics for men and women:

$$ \ln(Y_m) =\hat\beta_m  \bar{X}_m $$

$$ \ln(Y_f) =\hat\beta_f  \bar{X}_f $$

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

The difference in average log earnings is:

$$ \ln(Y_m) - \ln(Y_f) = \hat\beta_m  \bar{X}_m - \hat\beta_f  \bar{X}_f $$

Add and subtract $\hat\beta_m  \bar{X}_f$:

$$ \ln(Y_m) - \ln(Y_f) = \underbrace{\hat\beta_m  (\bar{X}_m - \bar{X}_f)}_{\text{explained}} + \underbrace{\bar{X}_f (\hat\beta_m - \hat\beta_f)}_{\text{unexplained}} $$

- [Explained:]{.fg style="color: #555;"} holds slope constant at $\hat\beta_m$, looks at differences in average $X$
- [Unexplained:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} holds average characteristics constant at $\bar{X}_f$, looks at differences in slopes (returns)

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

::: {.callout-warning}
Traditionally, the [unexplained part is interpreted as discrimination]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} — but could also be due to unobserved productivity differences
:::

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

![](images/oaxaca.png){fig-align="center"}

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

Suppose we have run the following regression separately for men and women:

$$\ln Y  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Educ} + \beta_2 \text{Experience}$$

Estimated coefficients:

- [Men:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} $\beta^M = (2.0,\; 0.10,\; 0.02)$
- [Women:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} $\beta^F = (1.8,\; 0.08,\; 0.015)$

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

Mean observed characteristics:

- [Men:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} $\bar{\text{Educ}}_M = 14$, $\bar{\text{Exp}}_M = 15$
- [Women:]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} $\bar{\text{Educ}}_F = 13$, $\bar{\text{Exp}}_F = 12$

Average predicted log wage for men:

$$\bar{\ln Y}_M = 2.0 + 0.10 \cdot 14 + 0.02 \cdot 15 = 2.0 + 1.4 + 0.3 = 3.7$$

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

Average predicted log wage for women:

$$\bar{\ln Y}_F = 1.8 + 0.08 \cdot 13 + 0.015 \cdot 12 = 1.8 + 1.04 + 0.18 = 3.02$$

The wage gap is therefore:

$$\bar{\ln Y}_M - \bar{\ln Y}_F = 3.70 - 3.02 = 0.68$$

This says that the wage gap is about [0.68 log points — roughly 68% higher wages for men]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

We decompose: $\bar{\ln Y}_M - \bar{\ln Y}_F = \text{Explained} + \text{Unexplained}$

[Explained (due to characteristics):]{.fg style="color: #555;"}

$$\text{Explained} = (\bar{X}_M - \bar{X}_F)\beta^M$$

Differences in means: Education: $14 - 13 = 1$, Experience: $15 - 12 = 3$

$$\text{Explained} = 1 \cdot 0.10 + 3 \cdot 0.02 = 0.10 + 0.06 = 0.16$$

About $0.16$ log points of the gap are due to men having more education and experience.

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

[Unexplained (returns to characteristics):]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}

$$\text{Unexplained (slopes)} = \bar{X}_F \left(\beta_M - \beta_F\right)$$

Coefficient differences: Education: $0.10 - 0.08 = 0.02$, Experience: $0.02 - 0.015 = 0.005$

$$\text{Unexplained (slopes)} = 13 \cdot 0.02 + 12 \cdot 0.005 = 0.26 + 0.06 = 0.32$$

Intercept difference: $\beta_{0M} - \beta_{0F} = 2.0 - 1.8 = 0.20$

Total unexplained: $0.32 + 0.20 = 0.52$

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

::: {.callout-tip}
## Final Decomposition

$$0.68 = \underbrace{0.16}_{\text{explained (24\%)}} + \underbrace{0.52}_{\text{unexplained (76\%)}}$$

- [Explained ($0.16$, ~24%):]{.fg style="color: #555;"} due to men having higher average education and experience
- [Unexplained ($0.52$, ~76%):]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} due to different returns to characteristics and intercept differences
:::

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

Here is an example using real data from Canada:

- Labour Force Survey from September 2025
- Restricted to people aged 35–54 with wages > 0
- First examine summary statistics, then run a regular regression, then the decomposition

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(modelsummary)
library(oaxaca)


lfs <- read_csv("pub0925.csv") %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  mutate(age_12 = as.numeric(age_12),
         hrlyearn = hrlyearn/100,
         gender = fct_recode(as.factor(gender), "Men" = "1", "Women" = "2"),
         educ = fct_recode(as.factor(educ),"0-8 yrs" = "0", "Some HS" = "1", "HS Grad" = "2", "Some PS" = "3", "PS Diploma" = "4", "BA" = "5", ">BA" = "6"),
         prov = fct_recode(as.factor(prov), "NL" = "10", "PEI" = "11", "NS" = "12", "NB" = "13", "QC" = "24", "ON" = "35", "MB" = "46",
                           "SK" = "47", "AB" = "48", "BC" = "59"),
         female = gender == "Women") %>%
  filter(between(age_12, 5,8),
         hrlyearn > 0)


## Kernel density plot of male and female hourly earnings

ggplot(lfs, aes(x=hrlyearn, group = gender, colour = gender)) +
  geom_density() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Wage Distribution by Gender",
       subtitle = "Age 35-54, September 2025",
       x = "Hourly Earnings",
       y = "Density")
```

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

```{r}
ggplot(lfs, aes(x=log(hrlyearn), group = gender, colour = gender)) +
  geom_density() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Wage Distribution by Gender (Log Scale)",
       subtitle = "Age 35-54, September 2025",
       x = "Hourly Earnings",
       y = "Density")+
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = function(x) round(exp(x), 0)   # converts log wages → wages
  )

```

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

```{r}
ggplot(lfs, aes(x = educ, y = hrlyearn, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), outliers = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Schooling Level",
    y = "Wage",
    title = "Wage Distribution by Schooling and Gender",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

```

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

```{r}
ggplot(lfs, aes(x = as.factor(prov), y = hrlyearn, fill = gender)) +
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), outliers = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Schooling Level",
    y = "Wage",
    title = "Wage Distribution by Province and Gender",
    fill = "Gender"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

```{r}
m1 <- lm(hrlyearn ~ gender, data = lfs)
m2 <- lm(log(hrlyearn) ~ gender, data = lfs)
m3 <- lm(log(hrlyearn) ~ gender + as.factor(age_12) + educ + as.factor(marstat) + as.factor(immig) + as.factor(union) + as.factor(prov), data = lfs)

modelsummary(
  list("Wage" = m1, "Log Wage" = m2, "Log Wage (with Controls)" = m3),
  coef_map = c(
    "genderWomen" = "Women"   # only show this coefficient
  )
)
```

## Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

```{r}
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

oaxaca<- oaxaca(log(hrlyearn) ~  as.factor(age_12) + educ + as.factor(marstat) + as.factor(immig) + as.factor(union) + as.factor(prov)|female, data = lfs)

# Convert to data frame
overall_twofold <- as.data.frame(oaxaca$twofold$overall)

# Select the 0.5 weighting row (default symmetric decomposition)
row <- overall_twofold[overall_twofold$group.weight == 0.5, ]

# Build table WITHOUT standard errors
tab <- tibble(
  Component = c(
    "Overall Difference",
    "Explained (Endowments)",
    "Unexplained (Coefficients)"
  ),
  Estimate = c(
    row[["coef(explained)"]] + row[["coef(unexplained)"]],
    row[["coef(explained)"]],
    row[["coef(unexplained)"]]
  )
)

kable(tab, digits = 3)

```

## Collider Bias

- Sometimes researchers control for variables in a regression to adjust the wage gap
  - What is the gap if we hold constant age, education, experience, occupation, industry, hours worked, etc.?
- The idea is to compare people who are the same on all relevant characteristics

::: {.callout-warning}
## Collider Bias
[Collider bias:]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} controlling for certain variables (like occupation) can actually **create bias** in discrimination estimates if those variables are themselves outcomes of discrimination
:::

## Collider Bias

Example — the tech industry:

- Men and women have equal ability in the general population
- Women face discrimination in tech, so to get the job they must have [very high ability]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- Men can enter even with moderate ability
- If you look at the wage gap in tech jobs, it might appear to [favour women]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
  - In the same occupation, women will have higher ability because they had to overcome discrimination
  - Comparing men and women within occupation **creates** ability bias

## Collider Bias

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/google.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
This happened at [Google]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}:

- There was a complaint that women were being underpaid
- An analysis found that **men** were underpaid
- A perfect example of collider bias
  - They looked within jobs
  - Women of very high ability were selected into those jobs
  - Their wages were higher because of that
:::
::::::

## Collider Bias

How to avoid collider bias:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Best Practice
[Do not add variables that are outcomes of discrimination]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} to the regression

- [Occupation]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} is often an outcome of discrimination
- [Industry]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} may also be an outcome

Instead include only [predetermined characteristics]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}: things that are not affected by discrimination — mainly basic demographics, possibly education and experience
:::

# Additional Evidence on Gender Pay Gaps

## Introduction

- Significant statistical work has been done on this issue
  - Why? Its importance and availability of data
- We will briefly review some of the evidence here, with a focus on Canadian studies

## Evidence

Key findings:

- Women in Canada earn about [60% of what men earn]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} (unconditional gap)
- After controlling for characteristics, the gap [shrinks to about 85%]{.fg style="color: #555;"}
- [Pay gap is smaller in the public sector]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} — pay practices are more egalitarian in government
- Gap has been [falling over time]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} — many factors could contribute
- Internationally, gaps are [smaller with stronger bargaining structures]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- Gap is [smaller the more competitive the industry]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}

## Evidence

Additional findings:

- [Occupational segregation does not explain a large part of the gap]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Gap is explained more by *industry* than occupation
- Women face [career penalties from family responsibilities]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
- [Glass ceilings]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} are an observed phenomenon
  - At the top end of the pay distribution, gaps are larger
  - Lots of international evidence of differences in career advancement
- [Unions have a higher impact on women than men]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Offset by the fact that women are less likely to be unionized

## Evidence

- [Mixed evidence on job-protected leave]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Leave is good because it protects jobs for women
  - But might make employers less likely to hire women in the first place
  - Evidence shows it [lowers wages for women in the U.S.]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - In Canada it [increases job continuity]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
- Some evidence that [gap grows with more work experience]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
  - Upon initial entry, gap is small
  - Grows over time

# Other Groups

## Introduction

- The same techniques used to analyze gender wage gaps can be used to estimate gaps for other groups
- This is usually done by [race or ethnicity]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - U.S. studies have focused in particular on racial discrimination

## Evidence for Other Groups

[Indigenous peoples in Canada]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}:

- About [85% of non-Indigenous wages]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} off reserve
- Shrinks after controlling for characteristics

[Ethnic-white wage gaps in Canada]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}:

- Complicated by the fact that many non-white Canadians are also immigrants
- Immigration has its own independent effect on wages
- Controlling for this, gaps are very high — summarized on next slide

## Evidence for Other Groups

![](images/ben54842_tb1201.jpg){fig-align="center"}

## Evidence for Other Groups

[Evidence in the U.S.:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Large literature on [Black-white wage gaps]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} — about 68% of white wages
  - Shrinks when controlling for past test scores (measure of pre-market productivity)
  - Pre-market discrimination also plays a large role
  - Large component of discrimination remains
- Gaps [favour Chinese and Southeast Asian workers]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} — not the same in Canada

# Policies to Combat Gender Discrimination

## Introduction

- Gender discrimination has been an issue for a long time
- Several policies are enacted to combat it:
  - [Equal pay]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - [Equal employment opportunity]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - [Policies to facilitate female employment]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

## Equal Pay

[Pay equity:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} requires that jobs which are substantially similar receive equal pay

- Looks at very similar jobs; minor differences are allowed
- Issue: deals with similar jobs in similar establishments — does not address equity issues across jobs/industries

[Equal pay for equal work:]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} broadens the scope

- Assigns points to jobs based on skill, effort, responsibility, working conditions
- Jobs with similar points should receive similar pay
- Can apply to different occupations, but still in same firm/industry

## Equal Pay

- Applies only to jobs that are predominantly male or female (>70%) — pay in female-dominated jobs adjusted to that of male-dominated jobs

## Equal Pay

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
![](images/payequity.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Equal pay for equal work example:

- Pay plotted against point scores
- In this example, male dominated jobs have generally higher pay
- Solutions could be:
  - Raise female line to male line
  - Raise female pay to male pay point-by-point for similar scores
  - Raise female points to male line at each point value
:::
::::::

## Equal Pay

::: {.callout-note}
Equal pay for equal work is based on [administrative concept of value]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} (points for skill, effort, responsibility, working conditions) — **not** based on economic (market) value

- This is purposeful: market value reflects discrimination; administrative value tries to remove this
:::

## Equal Employment Opportunity

- [Equal pay]{.fg style="color: #555;"} focused on equalizing wages
- [Equal employment opportunity]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} focuses on equalizing [access to jobs]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - But by equalizing access, we also expect wages to equalize
- Key initiative is [affirmative action]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} (aka employment equity)

## Equal Employment Opportunity

::: {.callout-important}
## Affirmative Action
Generally involves [preferential treatment for minority groups]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

- Intended to overcome past and current discrimination
- Designed to be used temporarily to restore balance

In Canada:

- Applies only to federal workforce (~10% of jobs)
- Applies to four targeted groups: women, visible minorities, disabled persons, indigenous peoples
- [Continues to be very controversial]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"}
:::

## Facilitating Policies

Finally, there are policies that can help [facilitate women in the workforce]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}:

- [Parental leave]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- [Child care subsidies]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- [Flexible work arrangements]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}

Canada has done well on the first two — expansion of child care subsidies recently is a good example

## Facilitating Policies

- Some consider [expanding unionization]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} to be a facilitating policy
  - Unions bargain for greater pay and working conditions
  - Expanding this to cover more women would help
  - May also generate more power for women to argue for other types of legislation

- [Removing pay secrecy]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} can also help
  - If employees know what others are paid, they can better negotiate
  - Pay secrecy tends to hide discrimination
  - Some jurisdictions have passed laws banning pay secrecy

## Preference and Attitudes

- We saw that discrimination in part is due to [preferences and attitudes]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
  - Taste-based discrimination is one example
- Could use public policy to try to change these attitudes:
  - Public awareness campaigns
  - Education programs
- Not clear how well this works

# Impact of Policies

## Introduction

- We have outlined the different anti-discrimination policies
- How effective are these policies?
- Relatively straightforward to analyze statistically
  - Use Program Evaluation techniques
  - Data generally available

## Pay Equity

::: {.callout-note}
## Pay Equity Effectiveness
- Generally [ineffective]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} in closing the gender gap
- Some evidence of an impact in the UK
- In the U.S., pay equity is difficult to disentangle from other civil rights legislation — effects are inconclusive
:::

## Equal Pay for Equal Work

- Analyzed mostly in the [public sector]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"}
- Recall the legislation is limited in scope
  - Male/female dominated jobs in same firm/industry
- Policy shown to close about [one-third of the gender gap in the public sector]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
  - Limited evidence in the private sector

## Affirmative Action

- Affirmative action is most prominent in the U.S.
- Several studies have examined its effect:
  - [Evidence that it helped employment opportunities of Black men]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
    - Were the main targets of the legislation in earlier years
  - In later years, [helped both Black men and women]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"}
    - Targets were expanded in later years

## Facilitating Policies

::: {.callout-note}
## Evidence on Facilitating Policies
- [Parental leave]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} policies help create job continuity
- [Subsidized child care]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} increases female labour force participation — good evidence from Quebec
- [Pay transparency]{.fg style="color: #5cb85c;"} reduces the gender gap by about 30% in academia — using evidence from the "sunshine list" in Ontario
- ["Tenure clock stopping"]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} policies reduce tenure rates for women — unintended consequence: men can increase productivity
- [Banning criminal history questions]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} hurt employment of Black men — increased use of discrimination
:::

# Summary

## Summary

- [Discrimination can arise from]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} tastes (Becker), statistical discrimination, supply-side factors, and non-competitive markets
- [Measuring discrimination is difficult]{.fg style="color: #2780e3;"} because productivity is not observed
  - Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition is a common method
- [Collider bias]{.fg style="color: #c7254e;"} is a potential issue when controlling for variables that are themselves outcomes of discrimination
- There are a number of initiatives to reduce discrimination
  - [Mixed evidence on their effectiveness]{.fg style="color: #555;"}
